title: Stroke: damage and the recovery of movement
description: In an ischaemic stroke an artery is blocked and part of the brain loses its blood supply. Where that happens varies from person to person, so the damaged area itself is not drawn. The episode follows one common situation: a stroke that weakens one hand. The studies pooled strokes on either side; it is drawn in the left half of the brain, weakening the right hand, for illustration. What is drawn is how the movement system works when the person tries to move that hand, compared with a healthy person moving theirs, from the first weeks through recovery over months.
caveat: Brightness here is activity while the weakened hand moves, compared with healthy people moving their hand; it is not activity at rest. The pooled analysis behind it combines many small studies with different tasks and degrees of weakness. The two studies that followed recovery included only people whose primary movement area was spared. The first two phases draw nothing, because where the damage falls varies and the distant effects of a stroke on connected areas are described in the sources without a direction that could be shown. Recovery differs a great deal between people, and the pattern shown is for recovery that goes well.

phases.name: An artery is blocked
phases.caption: An artery is blocked and part of the brain loses its blood supply. For a large stroke that goes untreated, researchers estimate an average loss of about 1.9 million nerve cells a minute, which is why stroke is treated as an emergency. Where the damage falls varies, so it is not drawn.

phases.name: Effects at a distance
phases.timescale: after the damage (timing not studied here)
phases.caption: Areas far from the damage can also change how they work and how they connect with each other. This is called diaschisis. The sources describe it without a direction that could be drawn.

order.rationale: Distant effects follow the damage by definition. When they appear and how long they last were not timed in the sources read.

phases.name: Working harder
phases.caption: When the person tries to move the weak hand, more of the movement system is active than in a healthy person: the movement cortex on the undamaged side and the supplementary motor area on both sides. The less complete the recovery, the more extra areas are recruited.

order.rationale: The pooled analysis combines patients scanned at different times after stroke. That the extra activity is greatest in the early weeks rests on it decreasing over time in the same analysis and in the longitudinal study.

phases.name: Recovery
phases.caption: As movement recovers, the extra activity falls back towards a healthy pattern. Good recovery goes with relying on the original movement network on the damaged side, rather than on the undamaged side.

citations.authors: Ward NS, Brown MM, Thompson AJ, Frackowiak RS
citations.title: Neural correlates of motor recovery after stroke: a longitudinal fMRI study.
citations.quote: consistent decreases across sessions correlating with recovery were seen across the whole patient group independent of rate of recovery or initial severity, in primary motor cortex, premotor and prefrontal cortex, supplementary motor areas, cingulate sulcus, temporal lobe, striate cortex, cerebellum, thalamus and basal ganglia

regions.explanation: The movement cortex on the undamaged side. It is more active than in healthy people when the weakened hand moves, a highly consistent finding across studies. That this extra activity decreases as movement recovers comes from one study that followed eight patients, which reports it for the primary motor cortex without naming the side. Good recovery goes with relying less on this side. The finding also covers the premotor cortex, which lies just in front of the area drawn.

regions.explanation: Drawn at the healthy level. Studies link the cerebellum to recovery in opposite ways: in one, people with poorer recovery showed more activity here; a pooled analysis links better movement to activity in the cerebellum. Neither finds it raised on average, and well-recovered patients show a normal pattern.
